<reason>Both sides were strong, but CON did the more decisive comparative work. CON repeatedly reversed PRO's best assets: the "welfare states layer cash on top" concession was flipped into an argument that uniform services fail outliers and that needing a cash patch concedes the motion's "rather than" framing; PRO's centerpiece asymmetry ("public worst day is degraded service, cash worst day is zero") was dismantled by the observation that planners abandon thin markets too — rural bus lines are cut first — so both systems can deliver zero, and the cash holder at least retains exit. CON also cleanly distinguished the fire department (rare, standardized) from recurrent, individualized needs like childcare and therapy, and distinguished network goods from personal care to blunt the roads/libraries analogy; PRO never squarely answered either. PRO's closing "visible and corrigible vs. invisible market failure" was a genuine recovery, but it leaned on an asserted political-pressure mechanism that CON had already characterized as a coarse, bundled signal, and PRO largely repeated the layering argument without engaging CON's reframe of it. Both openings/rebuttals were clipped once, roughly offsetting execution costs. CON's consistent targeting of the motion as written and sharper crystallization ("trust the household, not the map") gave a clear but competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1–B4.6: CON flipped PRO's prized concession ([B2.2] layering) into evidence that services need cash as a patch, then destroyed PRO's degraded-vs-zero asymmetry by showing public planners abandon thin markets too, leaving the cash holder with agency and exit while the service captive has only the complaint line.</best_rebuttal>
